title: Wesley's journal
hook: 24 May 1738: someone reading Luther's preface to Romans, and a warmed heart
tomorrow: who would ever ask God to put them to suffering?

segments.voice: Yesterday Bunyan's pilgrim crossed the river, scars and all, and the trumpets sounded. Today, a real diary, and one evening its writer never forgot.

Before-and-after posts. The day I quit. The day everything changed. People love a story with a timestamp. Christians have one too, and they argue, kindly, about what it means. John Wesley, an Anglican priest who would go on to start the Methodist movement, went to a meeting he didn't want to attend. And his journal records exactly what happened at a quarter to nine.
screen: `THE DAY EVERYTHING CHANGED.` → `A MEETING HE DIDN'T WANT.` → `A QUARTER TO NINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the entry for May 24, 1738. "In the evening I went very unwillingly to a society in Aldersgate Street." Someone there was reading Martin Luther's preface to Paul's letter to the Romans. About a quarter before nine, while the reader described the change God works in the heart through faith in Christ, Wesley writes: "I felt my heart strangely warmed." He says he trusted Christ alone, and was given assurance his sins were taken away, "even mine." Now the two views. One side says: this is what faith looks like. A night you can name, a heart you can feel, a date in the diary. Some Methodists and evangelical Christians tell their own stories with a moment like this, and it gives them something to come back to. The other side says: faith is mostly a long road, begun in baptism, grown in a church, in years of ordinary Sundays. And they can point to Wesley too. He had been a priest for years before that night. And in the same entry, he admits that doubts came back almost at once, and he prayed through them. So the warmed heart didn't end the road. Both sides can hold his journal and say: see?
screen: `VERY UNWILLINGLY, TO ALDERSGATE.` · `STRANGELY WARMED.` · `A NIGHT YOU CAN NAME.` · `OR A LONG ROAD OF SUNDAYS.` · then, large: `I FELT MY HEART.`

segments.voice: Read one line of Romans out loud, slowly, the letter Wesley was hearing about that night: "For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death." Read it a second time as if you'd never heard it. Then sit, and let whatever it stirs, or doesn't, be enough.
Wesley's journal. A priest's diary, one unwilling evening on Aldersgate Street, and a heart strangely warmed at a quarter to nine.
Your line: I felt my heart. Some faith has a timestamp, and some is a long road; Wesley's diary has room for both. Until tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Wesley's journal holds a night he could name, inside years as a priest and with doubts after. Christians tell faith both ways.
